Eight numbers per flow field: reduced-order models, a β-VAE and a latent-space design search

The same 489 RANS simulations as Part 1, now as whole fields. A linear and a nonlinear reduced model compress each field to eight numbers; a surrogate predicts them from the design parameters and a small head reads lift and drag from them. The chain screens 3,600 candidate airfoils, decodes the field of any design, and stands in for the coefficient surrogate inside the Part 1 control loop.

Objective

Part 1 turned 489 RANS simulations into a function of five design numbers that returns lift and drag, and trained a flap controller on it. That function knows nothing about the flow itself. This part asks whether the whole flow field can be compressed into a handful of numbers, whether those numbers can be predicted from the design parameters, and what that buys: a design search over thousands of candidate airfoils with a predicted field for each, and a second aerodynamic function for the controller of Part 1, built from the same simulations by a different route.

The work continues the numbering of Part 1:

  1. Stage 5 — Reduced-order models of the flow fields and a latent-space design search. Two reduced-order models of the fields, a linear one (proper orthogonal decomposition, POD) and a nonlinear one (a β-variational autoencoder, β-VAE), both at eight coordinates per field; a latent surrogate from the five parameters to those coordinates; an aerodynamic head from the coordinates to C_L and C_D; a design search; and the checks on how far the search can be trusted, including an ensemble, an interpretation of the latent space and the cost of a query.
  2. Stage 6 — The field model inside the flap-control loop. The Stage 5 chain placed in the Part 1 control environment in place of the coefficient surrogate, with PPO trained three times in each environment and every agent tested in both, plus the pressure field decoded along a controlled flight.

Problem statement

The data are the same 489 four-digit AirfRANS cases as Part 1, but now as fields: for each case, five channels (u/U∞, v/U∞, p/U∞², log(1 + νt/ν) and the signed distance to the surface, negative inside the body) interpolated onto one regular grid of 64 × 128 points covering −0.5 to 1.5 chords in x and −0.5 to 0.5 in y, with the same official split of 378 training and 111 test simulations and the same five parameters per case. A field is 40,960 numbers; the question is how few suffice.

Three questions follow. How few numbers describe a field, and does a nonlinear compression beat a linear one of the same size? Can those numbers be predicted from the design parameters well enough to screen designs by lift and drag? And which admissible four-digit design maximises C_L/C_D at a chosen operating point, and is that answer inside the region the models know? No flow solver is run: every result is a prediction checked against held-out simulations.

Method

Two reduced models at the same size

Each channel is standardised with training statistics. POD treats each scaled field, flattened to 40,960 values, as one snapshot and keeps the eight orthonormal patterns that carry the most variance; it is the best linear basis of that size, computed as a PCA. The β-VAE replaces the fixed patterns with two networks: a convolutional encoder (three stride-2 convolutions, 173,440 weights) that outputs a mean and a log-variance for each of eight coordinates, and a mirrored decoder (116,021 weights). Its loss is the reconstruction error plus β times the Kullback–Leibler term, with β raised linearly to 10⁻³ over the first 30 epochs as a guard against the coordinates collapsing to the prior; 100 epochs, Adam at 10⁻³, batch 32. For evaluation and as the surrogate's target the posterior mean μ is used, never a random sample.

From parameters to coordinates to forces

A latent surrogate (MLP 5 → 64 → 64 → 8, tanh) maps the scaled parameters (with log₁₀ Re) to the eight coordinates, one for POD and one for the β-VAE. An aerodynamic head (MLP 8 → 32 → 2, tanh) maps the coordinates to C_L and C_D; it is trained on the coordinates of the true training fields and used on predicted ones, which is the cost measured in question 5. Both are trained with 15 % of the training rows held out for early stopping, latent targets divided by one global scale so the POD coordinates keep their energy ordering, and the head's inputs and targets standardised because C_D is about a hundred times smaller than C_L. Where a result depends on an initialisation, it is repeated with three seeds.

Baselines

  • POD against the β-VAE at the same size, per channel, on the same 111 unseen fields; POD with 10, 20, 30 and 128 modes for perspective.
  • The training-mean coordinates and a linear fit against the latent surrogate, so that the surrogate's share of the error is measured against something.
  • A linear head, the mean of the training coefficients, and the Part 1 coefficient surrogate (five parameters straight to C_L, C_D, trained on the same 378 cases) against the aerodynamic head.

At eight coordinates the nonlinear model wins overall, 0.0375 against 0.0557, and the seed spread (0.0353 to 0.0397) is small next to the gap. It wins on the hard channels (u, pressure, turbulent viscosity) and loses on the two easiest (v and the signed distance), where a linear basis already does well. POD with 20 modes (0.0334) beats the β-VAE with eight, so the β-VAE is justified only because the models downstream need few coordinates.

Yes, within the training region. The β-VAE chain is the most accurate of the chains and slightly better than the Part 1 surrogate, which maps the five parameters straight to the coefficients with no field in between. The advantage (0.0212 against 0.0259) is about twice the seed spread and compares three runs with one model, so it is suggestive rather than established. The nonlinearity of the head matters for the β-VAE (a linear head gives 0.0450) and much less for POD, whose coordinates are already close to linear in the forces; the head on the true coordinates shows what the latent-surrogate step costs, about 0.0035 in C_L RMSE. The same eight numbers now serve the field and the forces.

All three models agree on a region, not on a design: thin, strongly cambered, camber in the front half. Every pick has t = 5.09 %, the thinnest section in the data, and the camber changes with the model and with the seed. Inside the box the predicted C_L/C_D rises toward thinner airfoils, so the search stops where the training data end, which is exactly where the models disagree most and where nothing has been tested.

By distance, neither optimum is an extrapolation: each is as close to a training case as a typical test case. But both sit on the boundary of the data in thickness, where the models disagree on the best camber and nothing was tested. Distance alone does not expose a boundary; the disagreement does, which is what the next section measures.

Results 4 — How far the search can be trusted

An ensemble over the design space

The spread is largest exactly where the optima sit. The median spread over the 3,600 candidates is 2.58 in C_L/C_D; at the three picks it is 6.95, 6.75 and 11.69, that is 2.6 to 4.5 times the median, in the 94th to 99.9th percentile of the grid. The median spread falls from 4.55 at t = 5.1 % to 2.04 at t = 19.9 %.

The ensemble cannot rank the top of the grid: its best candidate (m 5.5, p 5.0, t 5.09; 118.1 ± 5.6) has 46 others within one standard deviation of it. On unseen cases the spread is a flag, not an error bar: over the 111 test cases the ensemble standard deviation of C_L and the error of the ensemble mean have a Spearman correlation of 0.29, and the 20 % of cases with the largest spread carry 1.5 times the error of the rest. Averaging the three chains also lowers the C_L RMSE from 0.0212 to 0.0152.

The three chains share one β-VAE (seed 2026) and differ in the surrogate and the head, so this ensemble measures part of the model uncertainty. Varying the β-VAE as well is the obvious next step.

What the eight coordinates encode

All eight coordinates are active (spread across training fields 1.3 to 2.3, posterior σ 0.06 to 0.08, KL term per coordinate 3.9 to 5.1), so the β warm-up did its job. They are not independent (|r| up to 0.64 between μ₄ and μ₈), which is what β = 10⁻³ buys: good reconstruction and a loosely organised latent space. No coordinate tracks the Reynolds number, whose effect on these fields is small.

Results 5 — The field model inside the control loop (Stage 6)

Part 1 trained a flap controller in an environment whose steady lift and drag came from the coefficient surrogate. Stage 6 exchanges that one function for the β-VAE chain, with nothing else changed, and asks what changes in the control problem. The target lift is the zero-gust value of whichever function is in use: 0.7595 with the surrogate, 0.7483 with the chain. The chain runs as a NumPy forward pass that agrees with Keras to 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ and costs 0.014 ms per call against 0.011 ms for the surrogate, so the two routes cost the same per step.

The gap between training environments (at most 0.0002) is far smaller than the spread between seeds (up to 0.0018). The lower uncontrolled error in the chain environment follows from its smaller lift slope, 5.82 against 6.51 per radian.
Trained in → tested inLift RMSE (3 seeds)
surrogate → surrogate0.0095 ± 0.0006
surrogate → chain0.0106 ± 0.0004
chain → surrogate0.0096 ± 0.0016
chain → chain0.0104 ± 0.0018
no control0.150 / 0.140

Exchanging the function left the controller unchanged within the seed spread, with the equivalent angle between 4.35° and 5.57° in every flight, deep inside the trusted range. That is the result one would hope for, and also the reason it is not a validation: both functions were fitted to the same 378 cases and agree where the agent flies. What the chain adds is the field; what it cannot add is range.

Key observations

  1. Eight numbers are not many for these fields. 33 POD modes hold 95 % of the variance; at eight coordinates the β-VAE cuts the test error by a third, but POD with 20 modes is better still. The nonlinear model pays off only because the downstream models need few coordinates.
  2. The compression, not the surrogate, limits accuracy. A good latent predictor adds about 2 % to the field error; the linear fit adds 0.06 and the training mean 0.33 to 0.39. Improving the compression is the lever.
  3. Fields and forces from the same eight numbers. The β-VAE chain reaches C_L RMSE 0.0212 and C_D RMSE 0.00074 on 111 unseen cases, on a par with a surrogate trained directly on the coefficients, and it can also return the field.
  4. The design search finds a corner, not a design. All optima lie at the thinnest section in the data, the camber changes with model and seed, and the ensemble spread at the picks is 2.6 to 4.5 times the grid median. A solver run is the missing step.
  5. Distance to the data is not enough as a validity test. Both picks are as close to a training case as a typical test case, yet they sit on the boundary in thickness. Seed and model disagreement exposed what distance did not.
  6. The latent space is readable. All eight coordinates are active; two follow the angle of attack, two follow the thickness, none follows the Reynolds number, and the traversal panels show each one acting where the physics says it should.
  7. The field model works inside the control loop. Controllers trained with it match those trained with the coefficient surrogate within the seed spread, at the same cost per step, and the field can be decoded along the flight.

Conclusion

The project turned a database of 489 solved flows into a function: five design numbers in, a whole flow field and two force coefficients out, with every query costing a fraction of a millisecond once the models are built. Both reduced models work on unseen simulations; the β-VAE does better than POD at the same size, and the chain built on it predicts lift and drag about as well as a surrogate fitted directly to the coefficients, while keeping the field.

The same function carries the limits of its data. The design search ran into the edge of the training box, and the models disagree exactly there. That disagreement, measured with three seeds and an ensemble, turned out to be a more useful warning than the distance to the nearest training case. The workflow the two parts point to is: build the database once, search or control in the reduced space, and confirm the result with one solver run. The last step is the one not taken here.

Placed inside the Part 1 control environment, the field model did the job of the coefficient surrogate without a measurable change in the controller. Two pieces are missing before the field, and not only the coefficients, can respond to the control: a database with flap deflections as a sixth input, and a model that advances the latent state in time, which steady simulations cannot provide.
